chapters.title: 7. A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions

assets.topic: Halo Effect, Confirmation Bias, and WYSIATI as Coherence Mechanisms
assets.visual_frame_description: An evidence-sorting station shows three glowing bins labeled Halo Effect, Confirmation Bias, and WYSIATI. A conveyor belt feeds in six scenario cards, each showing a named person and a short workplace story: a manager sizing up a colleague, a professor grading essays, a memory question about a friend, a product lead running tests, a review board, and a leadership panel. The player drags each card into the bin whose mechanism best explains the outcome.
assets.player_mission: Read each scenario card and decide which of the three coherence mechanisms it demonstrates. Match the behavior to the mechanism the chapter names, and justify each placement from the evidence in the text.
key_concepts: The halo effect is the tendency to like or dislike everything about a person, including things you have not observed, and it plays a large role in shaping our view of people and situations.
The halo effect is one of the ways the representation of the world that System 1 generates is simpler and more coherent than the real thing.
Real evidence of generosity is missing in the story of Joan, and the gap is filled by a guess that fits one's emotional response to her.
The sequence in which we observe characteristics of a person is often determined by chance, yet sequence matters because the halo effect increases the weight of first impressions.

The operations of associative memory contribute to a general confirmation bias: when asked whether Sam is friendly, different instances of Sam's behavior come to mind than if you had been asked whether he is unfriendly.
A deliberate search for confirming evidence, known as positive test strategy, is how System 2 tests a hypothesis, contrary to the philosophers' advice to try to refute it.
WYSIATI, which stands for what you see is all there is, describes how System 1 is radically insensitive to both the quality and the quantity of information behind its impressions and intuitions.
The measure of success for System 1 is the coherence of the story it manages to create; the amount and quality of the data on which the story is based are largely irrelevant.
The combination of a coherence-seeking System 1 with a lazy System 2 implies that System 2 will endorse many intuitive beliefs that closely reflect the impressions generated by System 1.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three main coherence mechanisms of the chapter: the halo effect, which inflates the weight of first impressions of a person; confirmation bias, which biases memory and evidence search toward what is already believed; and WYSIATI, the radical insensitivity of System 1 to missing information. Kahneman shows all three make the world feel simpler and more coherent than it is, which is why a lazy System 2 so often endorses the resulting intuitions.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: For each scenario card, decide which mechanism best explains the outcome.
assets.column_a_label: Halo Effect (emotional coherence about a person)
assets.column_c_label: WYSIATI (what you see is all there is)

rows.label: A manager who liked a colleague's confident presentation now assumes the same colleague is punctual, fair, and generous
After a student's strong first essay, a professor gives the vague second essay the benefit of the doubt
Asked whether Sam is friendly, you retrieve instances of friendliness rather than instances of unfriendliness
A product lead designs tests that would confirm her new feature works rather than tests that could refute it
A review board that saw only the prosecution's account reports more confidence than a board that heard both sides
Hearing that Mindik is intelligent and strong, you answer that she will be a good leader without asking what you would need to know

distractors: Anchoring, because the first piece of information biases later estimates
Availability heuristic, because vivid cases come to mind easily
Regression to the mean, because extreme first impressions average out
assets.explanation: The halo-effect rows spread one positive impression to unobserved traits and give later information the benefit of the doubt; the confirmation-bias rows show memory and test design slanted toward what is already believed; the WYSIATI rows show confident judgments formed from partial, one-sided evidence with no allowance for what is missing.

assets.topic: Suppression of Ambiguity, Framing, and Base-Rate Neglect
assets.visual_frame_description: A museum-style exhibit wall presents three panels labeled Suppression of Ambiguity, Framing Effects, and Base-Rate Neglect. Six evidence cards float in front of the wall, each illustrating a finding: the A B C and 12 13 14 display, the word bank, a surgeon's survival statistic, a fat-free label, and a meek tidy stranger. The player routes each card to the panel it best demonstrates.
assets.player_mission: Classify each exhibit into the bias it demonstrates. Read the card, recall how the chapter presents each example, and decide whether it is about resolving ambiguity, reacting to a single formulation, or letting vivid individual description override statistical facts.
key_concepts: The middle shapes in the A B C and 12 13 14 displays are identical, but you read them as letters in a context of letters and as numbers in a context of numbers.
The word bank is ambiguous: without an explicit context, System 1 generated a likely context on its own, and you were not aware of the choice or of the possibility of another interpretation.
System 1 does not keep track of alternatives that it rejects, or even of the fact that there were alternatives; conscious doubt is not in its repertoire.
The statement that the odds of survival one month after surgery are 90 percent is more reassuring than the equivalent statement that mortality within one month is 10 percent.
Cold cuts described as 90 percent fat-free are more attractive than when they are described as 10 percent fat.
The equivalence of the alternative formulations is transparent, but an individual normally sees only one formulation, and what she sees is all there is.
Steve, the meek and tidy soul, is often believed to be a librarian even though you surely know that there are more male farmers than male librarians.
The personality description of Steve is salient and vivid, and the statistical fact about farmers almost certainly did not come to mind when you first considered the question.
Framing effects arise because different ways of presenting the same information often evoke different emotions.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests three biases that Kahneman traces to the same System 1 machinery: the suppression of ambiguity, framing effects, and base-rate neglect. Each demonstrates that what we see is all there is, because System 1 resolves ambiguity without awareness, reacts to the single formulation before it, and lets vivid individual descriptions override statistical facts.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: Assign each exhibit card to the bias it best demonstrates.

rows.label: The same middle shape is read as B among letters and as 13 among numbers, without awareness of the ambiguity
Without context, the word bank conjures money and tellers, and you never notice that another interpretation was possible
The odds of survival one month after surgery are 90 percent feels more reassuring than mortality within one month is 10 percent
Cold cuts described as 90 percent fat-free are more attractive than the same product described as 10 percent fat
Steve, meek and tidy, is judged likely to be a librarian even though there are far more male farmers than male librarians
A politely dressed stranger carrying a hardcover book is assumed to be a writer, though writing is a far rarer occupation than the trades around him

distractors: Halo effect, because one trait colors all judgments of a person
Anchoring, because the first number considered dominates the estimate
Mere exposure, because repeated exposure increases liking
assets.explanation: The ambiguity cards show System 1 settling on a single interpretation without registering that alternatives existed. The framing cards show equivalent descriptions evoking different emotions because only one formulation is seen. The base-rate cards show a vivid individual description crowding out the statistical fact that should govern the judgment.

assets.topic: Independent Judgments, Shared Bias, and First-Impression Contamination
assets.visual_frame_description: A meeting-room simulation shows three zones on a whiteboard: Independent Judgments, Correlated Judgments, and Halo-Effect Contamination. Six activity cards float in, depicting a penny-jar contest, two witnesses chatting before testifying, an open committee discussion, a professor grading booklets, and a row of scorecards. The player sorts each card into the zone that describes how the judgments behave.
assets.player_mission: Sort each activity by how its errors behave. Use the chapter's principle of decorrelated errors to tell apart independent judgments that cancel errors, shared biases that resist aggregation, and sequential judgments contaminated by a first impression.
key_concepts: When many people estimate the pennies in a jar, individuals do very poorly, but pools of individual judgments do remarkably well.
The errors that individuals make are independent of the errors made by others and, in the absence of a systematic bias, they tend to average to zero.
If the observers share a bias, the aggregation of judgments will not reduce it.
Allowing the observers to influence each other effectively reduces the size of the sample, and with it the precision of the group estimate.
Good police procedure keeps multiple witnesses from discussing an event before testifying, so that unbiased witnesses do not influence each other.
A simple rule for meetings is that before an issue is discussed, all members of the committee should write a very brief summary of their position.
The standard practice of open discussion gives too much weight to the opinions of those who speak early and assertively, causing others to line up behind them.
Kahneman found that when he scored the first essay before the rest, that question had a disproportionate effect on the overall grade, a halo effect.
When he switched to scoring all answers to one question before the next, his grades for a single student often varied over a considerable range.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the principle of decorrelated errors: independent judgments with independent errors average to accurate estimates, while shared bias and mutual influence preserve or inflate error. Kahneman argues that the halo effect contaminates sequential judgments, so the remedy is to make observations independent before aggregating them.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: Sort each activity card into the zone that best describes how its judgments and errors behave.
assets.column_c_label: Halo-Effect Contamination (first impression distorts later judgments)

rows.label: Many people privately estimate the pennies in a jar, and the averaged estimates are remarkably accurate
Witnesses who discuss the event before testifying end up sharing the same errors, reducing the value of their testimony
In an open committee, members line up behind the first person who speaks early and assertively
Observers who share a common bias produce an average estimate that is just as biased as any single judgment
A professor who scores a student's strong first essay then gives the same student's weak second essay the benefit of the doubt
Scoring all students' answers to question one before reading any question two makes each student's grades vary across a wide range

distractors: Only a laboratory curiosity with no real-world application
A proof that group judgment is always worse than individual judgment
A phenomenon caused exclusively by personality traits
assets.explanation: Private, independent estimates have uncorrelated errors that average toward accuracy, and scoring all answers to one question first removes contamination. The witness chat, the open committee, and the shared bias all make errors correlated, so aggregation cannot reduce them. The professor who lets the first essay color the second is the chapter's own halo-effect example.

assets.topic: The One-Sided Case: Confidence Without Evidence
assets.visual_frame_description: A corporate investigation room with a single wall clock; Theo, a regional operations manager in a gray suit, sits behind a desk with one thin report open. A colleague stands across from him holding a second folder. On the right, a confidence meter shows a high, steady reading, and a transcript panel scrolls Theo's answers.
assets.player_mission: Audit Theo's confident ruling in a workplace complaint case. Decide whether his certainty reflects deliberate deception, accurate expertise, or the one-sided-evidence effect, and issue the correct diagnosis using the chapter's legal-scenario findings.
key_concepts: Participants who were exposed to one-sided evidence were more confident of their judgments than those who saw both sides.
The confidence that people experience is determined by the coherence of the story they manage to construct from available information.
It is the consistency of the information that matters for a good story, not its completeness.
Knowing little often makes it easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern.
The lawyers in the study added no useful information that you could not infer from the background story, yet one-sided presentation had a pronounced effect.
WYSIATI, what you see is all there is, explains why neither the quantity nor the quality of evidence counts for much in subjective confidence.
We often fail to allow for the possibility that evidence that should be critical to our judgment is missing.
The associative system tends to settle on a coherent pattern of activation and suppresses doubt and ambiguity.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests WYSIATI and one-sided evidence: Theo's confidence comes from the coherence of a single consistent story, not from the completeness of the evidence. Kahneman's legal scenario showed that people given one-sided evidence are more confident than those who heard both sides, because confidence tracks story coherence, not data quality.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: What is the correct diagnosis of Theo's confident ruling in favor of the store manager?
assets.subject_baseline: Theo is a meticulous regional manager with twenty years of experience who prides himself on reading every document twice; in past reviews he has often changed his position after hearing the other side, and his colleagues call him even-handed.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 14:05 — Theo states his conclusion within seconds of being asked, arms crossed, tone flat and certain. 14:08 — Asked whether he considered the union representative's account, he gestures to the single report on his desk and says the manager's version is consistent. 14:11 — When pressed to imagine the other side's argument, he shrugs, looks away briefly, then repeats his conclusion with unchanged confidence. 14:15 — No classic deception cues: no sweating, no long pauses, no contradictions; his confidence simply does not waver.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Colleague: What is your ruling? Theo: The manager acted properly. He gave the union man a lawful choice, and the arrest followed a refusal. Colleague: Did you read the union representative's statement? Theo: I do not need it. The manager's account hangs together; every detail supports every other. Colleague: Your colleague who read both accounts came to the opposite conclusion. Theo: She sat with too much information. The more I read, the less sure I felt, and that is not a good sign.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Not deliberate deception — Theo's high confidence is a product of one-sided evidence: he constructed a coherent story from a single account, and coherence, not completeness, drove his confidence (WYSIATI).
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Theo exhibits the exact pattern from the chapter's legal study: participants who saw only one side were more confident than those who saw both, because confidence depends on the coherence of the story that can be constructed from available information. His remark that more reading made him less sure is the WYSIATI signature, and the absence of deception cues confirms that the belief is genuine rather than manufactured.
distractors: Deliberate deception to protect a favored store manager
Accurate judgment from superior expertise in retail operations
Emotional bias from personal dislike of union representatives

assets.topic: The Depleted Believer: System 2 Too Busy to Unbelieve
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim compliance office late in the evening; Lena, a compliance analyst in a rumpled cardigan, slumps at her desk under a wall of sticky notes. A manager stands beside her holding a printed chain email. On the right, a fatigue tracker shows a full day of audit sessions, and a transcript panel records Lena's flat, certain answers.
assets.player_mission: Audit Lena's insistence that a vendor-tampering rumor is a verified fact. Determine whether she is lying, accurately recalling a document, or demonstrating the bias to believe under depletion, and issue the correct diagnosis.
key_concepts: Daniel Gilbert proposed that understanding a statement must begin with an attempt to believe it; only then can you decide whether or not to unbelieve it.
Gilbert sees unbelief as an operation of System 2, which is in charge of doubting and unbelieving but is sometimes busy and often lazy.
In Gilbert's experiment, participants who held digits in memory during the task had difficulty unbeliving false sentences.
In a later memory test, the depleted participants ended up thinking that many of the false sentences were true.
When System 2 is otherwise engaged, we will believe almost anything; System 1 is gullible and biased to believe.
Even a nonsensical statement will evoke initial belief, as when whitefish eat candy produced vague impressions of fish and candy.
People are more likely to be influenced by empty persuasive messages, such as commercials, when they are tired and depleted.
The initial attempt to believe is an automatic operation of System 1, which involves the construction of the best possible interpretation of the situation.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the bias to believe described by Daniel Gilbert: understanding begins with an automatic attempt to believe, and unbelief is a System 2 operation. When System 2 is busy or depleted, we fail to unbelieve false statements and later treat them as true, which is why Lena remembers the rumor as fact.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: What is the correct diagnosis of Lena's insistence that the vendor-tampering claim is a verified fact?
assets.subject_baseline: Lena is a careful compliance analyst who normally double-checks source documents before asserting anything; in her first six months she was praised for flagging two genuine discrepancies and for refusing to speculate.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 21:40 — Lena states the tampering claim as fact on the first mention, eyes unfocused, voice low and flat, shoulders slumped. 21:44 — Asked where she saw it, she hesitates, scrolls her inbox, and says she saw it somewhere, maybe in the afternoon meeting. 21:48 — Told that the claim came from a chain email, she frowns, appears genuinely puzzled, and says that cannot be because she remembers it being true. 21:52 — No evasion cues; her affect is exhaustion, not alertness, and she seems unable to trace the source of her own belief.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Manager: You stated the vendor tampered with the invoice as a confirmed fact. Lena: It is confirmed. I am sure I saw it. Manager: Where was that confirmed? Lena: I do not remember exactly, but I am sure it is true. Manager: You were in a three-hour audit session when that email went around, holding figures in your head the whole time. Lena: Maybe. I do not remember that part. But the claim is true; I remember it as true.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Not deliberate deception — Lena is experiencing the bias to believe: her System 2 was otherwise engaged during a demanding task, so she failed to unbelieve a false statement and now remembers it as true.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Gilbert's experiment showed that when System 2 is disrupted, people have difficulty unbeliving false sentences and later misremember them as true; Lena's story mirrors this exactly, since she was holding figures in memory at the very moment the claim reached her. Her inability to trace the source while insisting on truth is the signature of a depleted, gullible System 1, and her flat, exhausted affect shows no classic deception cues.
distractors: Deliberate cover-up because Lena helped tamper with the invoice
Accurate recollection of a documented fraud she reviewed
A random guess made under time pressure

assets.topic: Boss Battle: Breaking the Halo Effect in Hiring
assets.visual_frame_description: A sunlit hiring suite at a design studio; three panelists interview a single candidate, Tomas, whose opening portfolio answer is brilliant. The panelists nod and smile, and from that moment every later answer is rated glowingly. A scoring sheet on the wall shows all six competencies marked at the same near-perfect level, and one panelist whispers that the candidate seems flawless.
assets.player_mission: Stop the panel from converting one strong first impression into a flawless scorecard. Identify the halo effect in action, then run the intervention that produces reliable, uncorrelated scores before the hiring decision is made.
key_concepts: The halo effect is the tendency to like or dislike everything about a person, including things you have not observed.
The halo effect increases the weight of first impressions, sometimes to the point that subsequent information is mostly wasted.
Kahneman found that when he gave a high score to a student's first essay, he gave the student the benefit of the doubt whenever he encountered a vague or ambiguous statement later on.
The consistency that came from reading each booklet in sequence was spurious and produced a feeling of cognitive ease, which his System 2 lazily accepted.
Kahneman's new procedure was to read and score all the students' answers to the first question before going on to the next, writing scores where they could not bias later reading.
Under the new procedure his grades for a single student often varied over a considerable range, and his confidence in his grading was much lower.
The procedure Kahneman adopted conforms to a general principle: decorrelate error.
If the observers share a bias, the aggregation of judgments will not reduce it.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests the halo effect in evaluation: one strong first impression inflates every later judgment, and the resulting consistency is spurious, producing a feeling of cognitive ease that a lazy System 2 accepts. The chapter's remedy is to decorrelate errors by scoring each dimension across candidates before discussing, which is exactly the intervention that defeats the halo in this panel.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is the halo effect in evaluation: once the interviewer is impressed by a strong first answer, the positive impression colors every later judgment, so the candidate gets the benefit of the doubt on everything else and the final rating becomes more coherent than the evidence justifies.
assets.stage_1_observation: In a sunlit hiring suite at a design studio, three panelists interview a single candidate, Tomas. His opening portfolio answer is brilliant, and the panelists nod and smile. From that moment each later answer is rated glowingly, and the final scoring sheet shows all six competencies at the same near-perfect level. One panelist whispers that the candidate seems flawless.
assets.stage_1_question: Why is the panel's near-uniform glowing scorecard so seductive, and what psychological mechanism is driving it?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The halo effect: the strong first impression led the panel to like everything about Tomas, including competencies they did not actually observe, so later information was mostly wasted and the scores became artificially homogeneous; the spurious consistency also produces cognitive ease, so a lazy System 2 accepts the final scorecard without noticing the missing evidence.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are the hiring lead and the panel is about to lock in final scores. Choose the intervention that most directly defeats the halo effect before the decision is made.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Decorrelation of errors: have each panelist score every candidate on a single competency before anyone moves to the next competency, with all scores written where they cannot contaminate later ratings and no discussion until every score is recorded, because Kahneman's grading change showed this procedure exposes real variability and removes first-impression contamination.

assets.topic: Boss Battle: Mindik's Two Adjectives (WYSIATI in Leadership)
assets.visual_frame_description: In a boardroom, the succession committee reviews a one-line candidate summary that reads: Sofia is intelligent and strong. The chair asks for a show of hands on leadership readiness, and nearly everyone raises a hand within seconds. A junior analyst in the corner starts to ask what other information they would need before judging, but the vote is already underway.
assets.player_mission: Stop the committee from converting two adjectives into a leadership verdict. Explain the WYSIATI trap, then force the committee to seek the information the story does not contain before any decision is finalized.
key_concepts: WYSIATI, which stands for what you see is all there is, describes how System 1 is radically insensitive to both the quality and the quantity of the information behind its impressions.
An essential design feature of the associative machine is that it represents only activated ideas; information that is not retrieved from memory might as well not exist.
The measure of success for System 1 is the coherence of the story it manages to create, while the amount and quality of the data on which the story is based are largely irrelevant.
When information is scarce, System 1 operates as a machine for jumping to conclusions.
On reading that Mindik is intelligent and strong, you answer that she will be a good leader without asking what you would need to know before forming an opinion about someone's leadership.
The best story that can be constructed from two adjectives is delivered with great cognitive ease, and there remains a bias favoring the first impression.
System 2 is capable of a more systematic approach to evidence, such as buying a home, when you deliberately seek information that you don't have.
Overconfidence follows from WYSIATI because neither the quantity nor the quality of evidence counts for much in subjective confidence.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests WYSIATI: System 1 constructs the most coherent story from activated information and is radically insensitive to both the quality and quantity of the missing evidence. Kahneman shows that jumping to conclusions from scant data feels easy and confident, and the only correction is a deliberate System 2 search for the information that the story does not contain.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is WYSIATI, what you see is all there is: System 1 builds the best possible story from the ideas currently activated and cannot allow for information it does not have, so a two-adjective description like intelligent and strong produces an instant, overconfident leadership verdict.
assets.stage_1_observation: In a boardroom, the succession committee reviews a one-line candidate summary that reads: Sofia is intelligent and strong. The chair asks for a show of hands on leadership readiness, and nearly everyone raises a hand within seconds. A junior analyst in the corner starts to ask what other information they would need before judging, but the vote is already underway.
assets.stage_1_question: What does the chapter say the board members failed to do before forming their opinion about Sofia's leadership?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: They never asked what they would need to know before forming an opinion: System 1 built the best possible story from the two adjectives and delivered it with cognitive ease, so the members jumped to a conclusion and retained a bias favoring that first impression, the pattern Kahneman describes with Mindik (WYSIATI).
assets.stage_2_intervention: The vote is about to be finalized. Choose the intervention that best forces the board to overcome WYSIATI before deciding.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Stop the vote and require the board to list the information they would need about Sofia's integrity, track record, and management results, then gather that evidence from independent sources before any judgment, because System 1 is radically insensitive to missing information and only a deliberate, checklist-driven System 2 can ask what the story leaves out.

assets.topic: Boss Battle: Killing the Rumor Machine (Confirmation Bias)
assets.visual_frame_description: In a crowded office kitchen, a rumor spreads that the company is being acquired and the local office will close. Within an hour, employees trade evidence: the CEO's calendar has a mystery meeting, a contractor asked about office space, two managers left early. Each new item is greeted as proof, and a whiteboard labeled Evidence fills up. An intern quietly asks what would disprove the rumor, and nobody can answer.
assets.player_mission: Defuse the rumor before morale collapses. Identify the confirmation machinery that keeps the evidence board growing, then run an intervention that forces the office to seek disconfirming evidence.
key_concepts: The operations of associative memory contribute to a general confirmation bias.
When asked whether Sam is friendly, different instances of Sam's behavior come to mind than if you had been asked whether he is unfriendly.
A deliberate search for confirming evidence, known as positive test strategy, is how System 2 tests a hypothesis.
Contrary to the rules of philosophers of science, who advise testing hypotheses by trying to refute them, people seek data that are likely to be compatible with the beliefs they currently hold.
The confirmatory bias of System 1 favors uncritical acceptance of suggestions.

If you are asked about the probability of a tsunami hitting California within the next thirty years, the images that come to mind are images of tsunamis, and you will be prone to overestimate the probability of a disaster.
When System 2 is otherwise engaged, we will believe almost anything; System 1 is gullible and biased to believe.
The combination of a coherence-seeking System 1 with a lazy System 2 implies that System 2 will endorse many intuitive beliefs.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests confirmation bias: people retrieve and seek evidence that matches the belief they already hold, and the confirmatory bias of System 1 favors uncritical acceptance of suggestions. Kahneman's positive-test-strategy analysis shows that a deliberate refutation test is the countermeasure to the rumor machine.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is confirmation bias and the positive test strategy: once a belief takes hold, associative memory retrieves confirming instances and people deliberately seek evidence compatible with what they already hold, rarely attempting to refute it.
assets.stage_1_observation: In a crowded office kitchen, a rumor spreads that the company is being acquired and the local office will close. Within an hour, employees trade evidence: the CEO's calendar has a mystery meeting, a contractor asked about office space, two managers left early. Each new item is greeted as proof, and a whiteboard labeled Evidence fills up. An intern quietly asks what would disprove the rumor, and nobody can answer.
assets.stage_1_question: Which mechanism from the chapter best explains why the rumor keeps accumulating confirming evidence?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Confirmation bias: associative memory retrieves instances compatible with the belief that the office will close, and the employees are using a positive test strategy, seeking data likely to confirm the rumor rather than trying to refute it, exactly as the chapter describes for the friendly-or-unfriendly Sam question.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are the office manager and need to calm the rumor before morale collapses. Choose the intervention most aligned with the chapter's analysis.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Force a search for disconfirming evidence: ask everyone to write down what would prove the rumor false, check each claim directly against its source, and obtain an independent, uncorrelated statement from the CEO, because the chapter shows people normally test hypotheses by seeking confirming data and a deliberate refutation test is the countermeasure.

assets.topic: Basic Assessments, Deliberate Computation, and Intensity Matching
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory console shows three compartments labeled Automatic Basic Assessment, Deliberate System 2 Computation, and Intensity Matching. Six task cards float in, each naming a mental act: evaluating a situation as good or bad, averaging a set of lines, counting capital letters, totaling a set of lines, and matching a sound's loudness to a crime's severity. The player routes each card to the compartment that describes how the mind performs it.
assets.player_mission: Classify each mental act by how the mind performs it. Use the chapter's distinction between the automatic basic assessments of System 1, the deliberate computations only System 2 can carry out, and the cross-dimensional matching that intensity scales make possible.
key_concepts: System 1 continuously monitors what is going on outside and inside the mind and generates assessments of various aspects of the situation without specific intention and with little or no effort.
Situations are constantly evaluated as good or bad, requiring escape or permitting approach.
Good mood and cognitive ease are the human equivalents of assessments of safety and familiarity.
A fraction of a second is sufficient for people to register the average length of an array of lines with considerable precision.
A glance provides an immediate impression of many features of a display, but you do not immediately know how many blocks are in a tower; that requires counting.

The only way to answer the total-length question is by activating System 2, which will laboriously estimate the average, estimate or count the lines, and multiply average length by the number of lines.
An underlying scale of intensity permits matching across diverse dimensions, because an underlying dimension of intensity allows the use of the word more.
In classic experiments, people adjusted the loudness of a sound to the severity of crimes, and other people adjusted loudness to the severity of legal punishments.
System 2 receives questions or generates them; in either case it directs attention and searches memory to find the answers.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the difference between the automatic basic assessments of System 1, the deliberate computations that only System 2 can perform, and the cross-dimensional matching that intensity scales make possible. The chapter shows that averages and similarities are computed automatically, sums require effort, and intensity matching lets System 1 translate between seemingly unrelated scales.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: For each mental act, decide which compartment best describes how the mind performs it.

rows.label: Continuously evaluating whether the current situation is good or bad, safe or threatening
Registering the average length of an array of lines within a fraction of a second
Counting the number of capital letters on a page
Estimating the total length of a set of lines by multiplying the average length by the number of lines
Matching the loudness of a sound to the severity of a crime so the punishment feels just
Judging how tall a man must be to be as remarkable as Julie reading fluently at age four

distractors: A process that only works for numbers and never for visual scenes
A process that requires conscious awareness to occur at all
A process governed by social norms rather than the individual mind
assets.explanation: Evaluating situations as good or bad and registering the average of a set of lines are automatic System 1 assessments; counting letters and totaling lengths are deliberate, effortful System 2 computations; matching a crime's severity to a sound's loudness and Julie's precocity to a man's height are cross-dimensional intensity matches.

assets.topic: Facial Competence, Substitution, and the Mental Shotgun
assets.visual_frame_description: A research theater shows three stage lights labeled Facial Competence Assessment, Substitution, and Mental Shotgun. Six finding cards float across the stage: a set of campaign portraits, a competence rating, a voter's decision, a GPA prediction, a rhyme test, and a sentence judgment. The player assigns each finding to the mechanism that best explains it.
assets.player_mission: Classify each finding by the System 1 mechanism it demonstrates. Read the card, recall the chapter's studies, and decide whether it shows an automatic facial assessment, the substitution of an easier question, or unintended excess computation.
key_concepts: Alex Todorov showed that a single glance at a stranger's face supports rapid judgments of how dominant and how trustworthy the person is.
The shape of the face provides the cues for assessing dominance, such as a strong square chin, and facial expression provides the cues for assessing the stranger's intentions.
In about 70 percent of the races for senator, congressman, and governor, the election winner was the candidate whose face had earned a higher rating of competence.
Todorov found that people judge competence by combining the two dimensions of strength and trustworthiness.
There is no evidence that these facial features actually predict how well politicians will perform in office.
The essential idea of the heuristics and biases approach is that basic assessments are easily substituted for more difficult questions.
System 1 can translate values across dimensions, as when you answer how tall Sam would be if he were as tall as he is intelligent.
The mental shotgun is the excess computation of System 1: an intention to answer a specific question automatically triggers other computations.
Listeners instructed to compare the sounds of VOTE and GOAT were slowed because they also compared the spelling, a superfluous computation that was detrimental to the main task.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario discriminates three features of System 1 in judgment: the automatic facial assessment of competence, the substitution of an easier question for a harder one, and the mental shotgun's excess computation. The chapter shows that all three operate without intention and influence judgments even when System 2 later makes the decision.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: Assign each finding card to the System 1 mechanism that best explains it.

rows.label: Princeton students rated competence from candidate faces shown for as little as one-tenth of a second and agreed strongly with one another
A face combining a strong chin and a slight confident smile is read as competent
A voter asked how well a candidate would perform in office instead answers how competent the face looks
Asked to predict Julie's college GPA from the age she learned to read, a predictor picks the GPA that matches her precocity
Listeners instructed to compare the sounds of VOTE and GOAT are slowed because they also compare the spelling
The sentence Some jobs are jails takes longer to reject because it is metaphorically true

distractors: Deliberate reasoning that requires conscious effort in every case
A deliberate strategy that people consciously choose to adopt
A purely social process that requires other people to be present
assets.explanation: Reading competence from a chin and smile and the one-tenth-of-a-second ratings are automatic facial assessments. Answering how the face looks instead of how well the candidate would govern, and matching Julie's GPA to her precocity, are substitutions. The spelling interference in the rhyme test and the metaphor interference in the sentence test are mental-shotgun computations that fired beyond the intended task.

assets.topic: The Face of Leadership: Reading Dominance in a Glance
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright interview suite at a law firm; Maria, a senior HR partner in a tailored blazer, sits opposite candidate Tomas. A colleague holds a file showing Tomas's team-turnover data. On the right, a facial-feature tracker highlights a strong chin and a slight smile, and a transcript panel records Maria's confident pronouncements.
assets.player_mission: Audit Maria's confident prediction that Tomas will be an outstanding leader. Decide whether her certainty reflects deliberate bias, expert judgment, or the automatic facial competence assessment described by Todorov, and issue the correct diagnosis.
key_concepts: Alex Todorov explored the biological roots of the rapid judgments of how safe it is to interact with a stranger.
We are endowed with an ability to evaluate, in a single glance at a stranger's face, how dominant and how trustworthy that person is.
The shape of the face provides the cues for assessing dominance, such as a strong square chin, and facial expression provides the cues for intentions.
Todorov found that people judge competence by combining the two dimensions of strength and trustworthiness.
The faces that exude competence combine a strong chin with a slight confident-appearing smile.
There is no evidence that these facial features actually predict how well politicians will perform in office.
Todorov showed that in about 70 percent of races, the election winner was the candidate whose face earned a higher competence rating.
The accuracy of face reading is far from perfect: round chins are not a reliable indicator of meekness, and smiles can to some extent be faked.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the automatic assessment of competence from faces: Maria reads dominance and trustworthiness in a glance and lets that quick impression override harder evidence. Todorov's research shows the mechanism shapes real decisions such as voting, even though facial features do not predict performance in office.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: What is the correct diagnosis of Maria's confident prediction that Tomas will be an outstanding leader?
assets.subject_baseline: Maria is a senior HR partner with eighteen years of experience who is known for structured interview rubrics and for demanding behavioral evidence; in previous selection panels she has twice vetoed candidates based on missing reference checks.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 10:15 — Within two minutes of meeting Tomas, Maria describes him as a natural leader, leaning forward with a bright smile. 10:20 — Asked what specifically signals leadership, she names his strong jawline, upright posture, and confident slight smile, gesturing to his face. 10:24 — When asked about his management results, she waves dismissively and says you can tell with some people in one glance. 10:28 — No signs of concealment; her confidence is warm and consistent, and she shows genuine surprise that anyone would doubt the read.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Colleague: What is your assessment of Tomas? Maria: He is the obvious choice. He looks like a leader. Colleague: What in his track record supports that? Maria: You can tell in one glance. Strong features, a calm smile; he projects competence. Colleague: But the data on his prior team shows high turnover. Maria: That will not matter. Some people simply look the part. I have always been able to read faces.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Not deliberate deception — Maria is relying on an automatic facial competence assessment (Todorov): she is reading dominance and trustworthiness from his face and substituting that quick impression for the harder judgment of leadership performance.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Todorov's studies show people evaluate dominance and trustworthiness in a single glance and combine them into a competence judgment, and this ancient mechanism influences even elections, yet there is no evidence that the facial features predict how well anyone performs in office. Maria's flat dismissal of track-record evidence, her appeal to looking the part, and the complete absence of deception cues mark this as a genuinely held System 1 assessment rather than a lie.
distractors: Deliberate bias to favor a candidate she already knows
Accurate expert judgment from two decades of leadership hiring
A moral judgment about Tomas's integrity

assets.topic: The Fixed Donation: A Prototype That Ignores Quantity
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright development office at a coastal wildlife nonprofit; Raymond, the development director, presents a bar chart to his colleagues. Three bars labeled 2,000 birds, 20,000 birds, and 200,000 birds all reach nearly the same height near eighty dollars. A video thumbnail of a struggling bird plays in a corner of the screen, and a transcript panel records Raymond's confident explanation.
assets.player_mission: Audit Raymond's claim that donor giving will not change when the number of birds saved changes. Decide whether he is manipulating numbers, describing a real marketing effect, or presenting the chapter's prototype effect on sum-like variables, and issue the correct diagnosis.
key_concepts: Participants asked their willingness to pay to save 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 birds gave average contributions of 80, 78, and 88 dollars respectively.
If saving birds is an economic good it should be a sum-like variable, and saving 200,000 birds should be worth much more than saving 2,000.
The number of birds made very little difference in the Exxon Valdez studies.
What the participants reacted to, in all three groups, was a prototype: the awful image of a helpless bird drowning, its feathers soaked in thick oil.
Because System 1 represents categories by a prototype or a set of typical exemplars, it deals well with averages but poorly with sums.
The size of the category, the number of instances it contains, tends to be ignored in judgments of sum-like variables.
The almost complete neglect of quantity in such emotional contexts has been confirmed many times.
System 1 has no suggestions to offer for the total length of a set of lines, and only System 2 can laboriously compute a sum.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the neglect of quantity in sum-like variables: willingness to pay did not grow from 2,000 to 200,000 birds saved because System 1 represents the category by a prototype, and the awful image of one drowning bird dominates the math. The chapter reports that the average contributions were 80, 78, and 88 dollars in the three groups.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.question: What is the correct diagnosis of Raymond's confidence that donor giving will stay flat no matter how many birds are saved?
assets.subject_baseline: Raymond is a seasoned development director at a coastal wildlife nonprofit who runs quarterly giving analyses and is known for preaching that donors respond to impact numbers; his reports are normally full of precise figures.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 13:05 — Raymond presents the mock giving data with pride, noting that 80, 78, and 88 dollars are nearly identical across the three scenarios. 13:09 — Asked whether a donor should pay more to save 200,000 birds than 2,000, he smiles and says people give to the picture, not the math. 13:12 — When pressed, he shrugs, cites the focus-group video of a struggling bird, and cannot articulate any mechanism besides the image. 13:15 — No deception cues; he is pleased, relaxed, and treats the result as a marketing insight rather than a problem.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Colleague: What did the giving test show? Raymond: We showed donors three versions: save 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 birds. The pledges were basically the same, about 80 dollars either way. Colleague: Should not 200,000 birds be worth a hundred times more than 2,000? Raymond: In theory, but people respond to one image: a helpless bird, feathers soaked in oil. That image is the story. Colleague: Are you saying the count is irrelevant to giving? Raymond: Yes. The bigger the number, the more it is just a number. The bird is what moves people.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Not deception — Raymond's donors are showing neglect of quantity in a sum-like variable: their willingness to pay was driven by the prototype of a single suffering bird, not by the number of birds saved, exactly as in the Exxon Valdez studies.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: In the chapter's example, contributions were 80, 78, and 88 dollars regardless of whether 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 birds would be saved, because participants reacted to the prototype of a helpless drowning bird. Raymond's focus-group insight that the image is the story is a faithful restatement of that mechanism, and his open, pleased demeanor with no deception cues indicates genuine belief rather than manipulation.
distractors: Deliberate fraud to inflate projected donations
A proven marketing strategy based on price anchoring
Donor apathy that has nothing to do with how the ask is framed

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Julie Problem (Prediction by Matching)
assets.visual_frame_description: In a university admissions office, three counselors review a file containing a single fact: Julie read fluently when she was four years old. Asked to predict her college GPA, they quickly agree on a near-perfect score because such early reading is so remarkable. A note on the wall reminds them that last year's early readers performed at or below average on the college measure.
assets.player_mission: Stop the office from converting a striking early achievement into an extreme prediction. Explain why prediction by matching is statistically wrong, then install a prediction process that replaces scale-matching with a sound statistical approach.
key_concepts: System 1 continuously generates basic assessments without specific intention, and these assessments are easily substituted for more difficult questions.
An underlying scale of intensity permits matching across diverse dimensions, allowing the use of the word more, as in more happy or more severe.
If crimes were colors, murder would be a deeper shade of red than theft, and if crimes were music, mass murder would be played fortissimo while parking tickets would be pianissimo.
In classic experiments, people adjusted the loudness of a sound to the severity of crimes, and other people adjusted loudness to the severity of punishments.
Julie read fluently when she was four years old, and you can match her precocity to a height, an income, a crime, or a GPA.
When people are asked to predict Julie's GPA from the age at which she learned to read, they answer by translating from one scale to another and pick the matching GPA.
This mode of prediction by matching is statistically wrong, although it is perfectly natural to System 1.
For most people except statisticians, prediction by matching is also acceptable to System 2.
System 2 receives questions or generates them, and in either case it directs attention and searches memory to find the answers.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests prediction by intensity matching: people answer the hard question of Julie's future GPA by translating her precocity into a matching value on another scale. Kahneman shows this feels natural to System 1 yet is statistically wrong, because matching ignores the imperfect relationship between the predictor and the outcome, and only statistical training makes System 2 reject it.

credibility.basis: Empirical behavioral economics research (Kahneman & Tversky; Nobel 2002)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is prediction by matching: when asked to predict a quantity such as Julie's college GPA from an early achievement such as reading at age four, people translate across dimensions and pick the value that matches in intensity, a mode that is natural to System 1 but statistically wrong because it ignores the imperfect relationship between the two variables.
assets.stage_1_observation: In a university admissions office, three counselors review a file containing a single fact: Julie read fluently when she was four years old. Asked to predict her college GPA, they quickly agree on a near-perfect score because such early reading is so remarkable. A note on the wall reminds them that last year's early readers performed at or below average on the college measure.
assets.stage_1_question: Why is the counselors' confident matching prediction statistically wrong even though it feels perfectly natural?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The prediction was produced by translating across intensity scales, matching how remarkable the reading was to an equally remarkable GPA, but the chapter states that this mode of prediction by matching is statistically wrong: the translation ignores that the relationship between the two measures is imperfect, so an extreme value on one scale should not imply an equally extreme value on the other.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The admissions director asks you to fix the prediction process before the decisions are sent. Choose the intervention that replaces matching with a sound statistical approach.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Use the actual historical relationship between early reading age and college GPA to produce the prediction, shrink extreme predictions toward the group average, and report a range rather than a single matched value, because the chapter shows matching is natural to System 1 but statistically wrong, and it is acceptable to System 2 only for people who are not trained to think statistically.
